content: Decorin is a protein encoded by the DCN gene in humans. It is classified as a proteoglycan with a molecular weight ranging from 90 to 140 kilodaltons (kDa). Decorin belongs to the small leucine-rich proteoglycan (SLRP) family and is composed of a protein core containing leucine-rich repeats, along with a glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chain. This GAG chain can be either chondroitin sulfate (CS) or dermatan sulfate (DS). Decorin is a small proteoglycan found in cellular or pericellular matrices and shares structural similarities with the protein biglycan. It is believed that decorin and biglycan arose from a gene duplication event. Decorin is a key component of connective tissue, where it binds to type I collagen fibrils and contributes to the assembly of the extracellular matrix. The name decorin is derived from its ability to decorate type I collagen fibrils and its interaction with the d and e bands of these fibrils. Decorin plays a significant role in fibrillogenesis, the process of collagen fibril formation. It also interacts with various other molecules, including fibronectin, thrombospondin, complement component C1q, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta). Decorin has been shown to modulate the activity of TGF-beta 1, either enhancing or inhibiting its effects. Its primary function is to regulate the cell cycle. Additionally, decorin is involved in the regulation of autophagy and endothelial cell function, and it acts as an inhibitor of angiogenesis. This anti-angiogenic effect is mediated through a high-affinity interaction with vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2), which leads to increased expression of the tumor suppressor gene PEG3. Decorin also inhibits other angiogenic growth factors, such as angiopoietin, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF). Recently, decorin has been identified as a myokine, a type of signaling molecule secreted by muscle cells. In this role, it promotes muscle hypertrophy by binding to and inhibiting myostatin, a negative regulator of muscle growth. Clinically, decorin expression is reduced in keloid scars compared to normal skin, suggesting its involvement in scar formation and wound healing. In animal studies, the infusion of decorin into rodent models of spinal cord injury has been shown to suppress scar formation and promote axonal growth. Decorin also exhibits anti-tumorigenic properties in experimental murine tumor models, where it suppresses the growth of various tumor cell lines. Mutations in the decorin gene are associated with congenital stromal corneal dystrophy, a rare genetic disorder affecting the cornea. Additionally, multiple alternatively spliced transcript variants of the decorin gene have been identified. Decorin interacts with several key molecules, including type I collagen, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), TGF-beta 1, Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2), and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). These interactions highlight its diverse roles in cellular and extracellular processes.
